chunks.text:
Hi Cairo,
I remember what it felt like. the airport, the paperwork, the particular silence of arriving somewhere that doesn’t know your name yet. i did it years ago: vietnam to canada, a teenager with a suitcase and a student visa and no real sense of what i was trading away. you did it this year. you packed a life into boxes and bet on yourself, and i watched from the other side of the screen, recognizing the shape of the thing even if the details were different.
There’s an immigrant’s arithmetic nobody warns you about. you leave your whole life back in Australia, and you trade a thousand small certainties for a handful of high-upside possibilities. the corner store that knew your order. the friends you could call without planning. the way your own vernacular and slang sat easy in your mouth, unremarkable, just there. you pay for every future friendship with a present loneliness. you buy a new life with a temporary loss of fluency in the invisible rules that make a day feel easy instead of expensive.
Edward Said wrote about exile as a “discontinuous state of being”: the self before and the self after, with a break between them that never fully heals1. i think that’s too dramatic for most of us. what i felt, and what i imagine you’re feeling, is something quieter: a thinning. the old life doesn’t disappear. it keeps running in the background threads, just harder to touch. you carry it like a photograph in a wallet, still yours, but flattened into something you look at instead of live inside.
To a wise man, the whole earth is open; for the native land of a good soul is the whole earth.Democritus, fragment 68 B247 (Diels–Kranz)
That line sounds noble until you’re actually doing it. the whole earth is open, sure, but belonging takes time. it takes the slow accumulation of references only locals understand, the moment when you stop translating in your head and just speak. you’re in the early phase of that accumulation now, and i want you to know: it compounds. the first year is the hardest. then one day you realize you’ve built something real without noticing the exact moment it became real.

From what i can tell, you’re doing well, in the sense of someone who is actually building. finding routines. finding people. learning a new place the way you learn a language, through the slow replacement of confusion with familiarity. that early phase, where every errand is research and every conversation costs extra attention, is its own form of work. the kind that doesn’t photograph well.
there’s a specific kind of strength in being a stranger and staying kind anyway. it would be easy to turn sharp, to treat the new place as hostile territory you’re just trying to survive. you didn’t do that. you stayed open even when openness was expensive. i noticed that, and i respect it.
Sebald’s emigrants are never quite at home, never quite foreign2. i don’t think it has to be that melancholy. some of us find a way to make the in-between feel like a place worth living. you seem to be doing that.

if you need anything (someone to just sit on the phone while you pace around your apartment at 2am because the time zones don’t line up with anyone else) i’m here. distance is just latency. you don’t have to do the whole thing alone, even when it feels like you do.
i know the weight of a suitcase. i know the weight of a dream that pulls you somewhere new. i’m glad you’re carrying both.

remarque


edward w. said, “reflections on exile” (granta, 1984). the essay is about the particular consciousness of the exile, neither fully here nor fully there, always aware of what’s been lost. ↩


w. g. sebald, the emigrants (1992; english 1996). four stories of displacement, memory, and the way the past keeps leaking into the present. ↩
